claims.text: The formation and persistence of a protective oxide on CrFeCoNiX alloys above 900 °C is primarily governed by the relative diffusion and oxidation kinetics of Cr, Al, Si, and Mn.
Al- or Si-containing CrFeCoNiX alloys form slower-growing, denser oxides than Mn-containing variants.
Mn diffuses more rapidly than the critical protective-oxide-forming elements in these alloys.
Rapid Mn diffusion disrupts oxide-scale uniformity and makes the scale prone to spallation.
During high-temperature exposure, Cr, Al, or Si diffuses to the alloy surface and selectively oxidizes.
Selective oxidation of Al or Si produces a continuous, slow-growing, adherent alumina or silica layer.
In Mn-containing alloys, higher Mn diffusivity causes rapid, heterogeneous oxide nucleation.
Heterogeneous oxide nucleation in Mn-containing alloys produces a less uniform scale that cracks and spalls.
The distribution and diffusion rates of Cr, Al, Si, and Mn mediate whether the resulting scale is dense and coherent or polycrystalline and cracked.
CrFeCoNiAl and CrFeCoNiSi alloys will develop more stable and coherent oxide scales than CrFeCoNiMn alloys under identical exposure conditions.
The Al- and Si-containing scales will have lower defect density and less spallation than scales on the Mn-containing alloy.
Oxide scales on the Al- or Si-containing alloys will be self-healing.
The proposed mechanism applies to single- or multiphase solid-solution CrFeCoNiX alloys during prolonged oxidative or corrosive exposure above 900 °C.
Diffusion rates and oxide kinetics are well established in simpler alloys.
Multiphase segregation may complicate oxide formation in these high-entropy alloys.

contradictions.description: The stated comparison is Al- or Si-containing alloys versus Mn-containing alloys, but the baseline is also described as CrFeCoNi without the Mn effect. CrFeCoNiAl and CrFeCoNiSi are modified alloys, not the unmodified CrFeCoNi baseline, so the baseline is inconsistently defined.
